chunk_findings.detail: The new release call is placed after the initial merge event is recorded but before the gitflow back-merge block. For a gitflow hotfix, the production merge can succeed, so `_release_at_merge` releases the item lease, and then the code attempts to back-merge the same branch to develop; if that back-merge fails (conflict, missing develop branch, etc.), the comment explicitly says the failure is reported rather than rolled back. At that point the lease is already gone, so a waiting agent can claim the files while the hotfix still needs exclusive access to retry or finish the back-merge. This contradicts the docstring and intent promise that a failed merge keeps the lease: the failure input is a gitflow hotfix whose production merge lands but whose develop back-merge fails.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/merge.py:_release_at_merge call site

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion intended to prove that the merge keeps the worktree is vacuous. `out` is the output of `claim T2`, which will contain a `worktree` key/path for T2's newly claimed worktree even if T1's worktree was deleted by the merge. Given a merge implementation that lands the commit and removes the source worktree, `tree.exists()` is false, but `"worktree" in out` is true, so the test passes despite violating the promise that the worktree and branch are kept for completion steps.

chunk_findings.detail: The knob-off test only checks that the item still has a truthy `lease` field after merge. It does not check that the globs remain held (for example, by asserting that `claim T2` is still refused) and it never calls `complete` to prove the lease is held "to complete". If `release_at_merge = false` leaves a stale lease object while dropping the actual glob hold, or if a later regression releases the lease during completion, this test still passes.

chunk_findings.detail: The change promises that the queue integrator also releases the lease and that tests cover "a merge via the queue releases too". This new test file contains only CLI `merge` tests; there is no test that a queue-integrated merge releases the lease or wakes a waiter. A queue path that uses a separate merge routine and forgets `_release_at_merge` would pass this suite.

chunk_findings.detail: The test fixture shells out to `git` directly with `subprocess.run`, bypassing the project's git port. [r-adapters] and the change's stated conformance rule that git is reached only through `infra.git` require external dependencies to go through a port; this makes the test depend on a git executable being present on `PATH` and prevents using the fake git adapter.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_release_at_merge.py:21

chunk_findings.detail: The new test helper invokes the real git binary directly with `subprocess.run(["git", "-C", ...], ...)`, bypassing the ddflow adapters port and using a subprocess instead of a fake. [r-adapters] requires external dependencies to go through a port and says tests use a fake instead of a subprocess. This makes the test depend on a real `git` on PATH and on the real filesystem/subprocess environment rather than the isolated adapter.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_release_at_merge.py:21 (in `_git`)

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert tree.exists() or "worktree" in out` does not actually verify that T1’s worktree is kept after merge. `out` is the output of the successful claim of T2, not T1, so if the implementation deletes T1’s worktree after the merge, `tree.exists()` is false, but the `or "worktree" in out` branch can still pass because the substitute `out` is T2’s claim output and can contain the word `"worktree"`. The test therefore misses the promised worktree retention.
